story_text.value: I'm building Clutterstrike. The first product is called Cluttersignal, which is a browser extension that gives users a second opinion on whether or not an email or link is safe or malicious without enterprise tooling right from their browser. I built it to help people identify scams and phishing attempts, even as those evolve into more sophisticated attacks and ideated it around both my parents, my family and friends, and colleagues. The hardest thing I am working on now is trying to find more edge cases that would slip by the screen to reduce the chance of false negatives as much as possible.

story_text.value:
Until recently I didn't understand what cold email really was and I accepted its price as one of those "it is what it is" things.

But exploring the topic, I realised that there is no reason someone should have to pay for cold email, so I built FlyHedwig.

With FlyHedwig you can manage hundreds of email addresses, schedule sending times, import lists, get stats... all the good stuff. Ah, and it's got some cool AI-classification and draft built in.

If you work with cold email, I'd love to hear your thoughts! And if you like the project, as it's OSS, starring it would help it reach more people and encourage me to continue to improve it!

story_text.value:
I wanted to share a lightweight mapping editor I’ve built to make it easier to improve MTB trail data on OpenStreetMap. In general MTB trails on OSM could be greatly improved, especially when it comes to IMBA ratings and I wanted to lower the barrier to entry to contributing to OSM.

Key features:

* Load satellite, lidar or OSM GPS traces to verify trail paths * Dedicated keybindings for quickly tagging a trail's IMBA rating and other actions * Add, edit and split trails to improve trail accuracy * Circle a group of trails to add or update a trail network * Load all trails in a given state or region (US and Canada supported to start) * Upload to OSM as a changeset

Hope some folks find this useful, let me know what feedback you have!

Hi, my name is Andrew and I'm the founder of mainbrella co. Just a few days ago Cloudflare launched their container sandbox service. We have no free plan (our base builder plan is $5 a month) but you are welcome to run the code in your own Cloudflare account.

The numbers are pretty good in terms of startup speed. First test we ran was: Create a fresh sandbox, get a usable shell 381 ms, 30 out of 30 tries worked the same speed. Then 100 simultaneous sandbox starts 680 ms avg 100 / 100 successful 100 distinct machines running at once!

Looking for feedback, feature requests and yes our first paying customers who we will cherish!

story_text.value:
Hey all - I made a thing with my clanker Kevin: Ototo (https://ototo.dev/) - yes this is clanker driven dev. The idea is to offload code exploration and other token'y heavy tasks to a smaller model to do the work and chuck the result back. This helps in a couple of ways (1) it saves tokens if you can offload to a cheaper or free local model (2) it can keep the main context clearer as it removes all the sherlocking thinking/exploration. It also saves more tokens than using anthropics own exploration agent.

I had originally played around with a graph based approach but found this to work better. Currently, I have this running with Qwen 3.8 27B on my framework (I had Kevin build me a custom inference engine to squeeze all the juice I could out of the AMD - https://gitlab.com/handmadedigital/projects/shocho).

It's been through a bunch of tests (results are available if people want) against a load of different repos, including comparing subsequent commits of large repos with claude, claude + exploration agent and claude + ototo and so far ototo seems to really help.

The site is very 'LLM'y at the moment - I haven't had time to edit it to make the text more readable for us humans. Sorry.

Hope it helps folks in their day-to-day.

--EOL

story_text.value:
Today marks 15 years since Steve Jobs died. I remember watching his narrated version of "Here’s to the crazy ones" that day and crying. It felt like he was reading his own obituary. The ad suddenly seemed to have been about him all along.

When I first saw the original as a teenager, I decided to buy a Mac. It took me four years of saving. I still think it’s the best ad ever made: it never mentions a product, but it sold me on the whole company.

To mark the anniversary, I recreated it as an animated monochrome experience that runs in the browser, with Jobs' original narration.

I used Claude Opus 5.5 (ultracode) for the code, animation, and sound design, GPT-Image-2.5 for the illustrations, and ElevenLabs for the music. The voice is Jobs’s actual recording, isolated from the original soundtrack.

story_text.value:
After I finished my job as a designer on Audacity 4, I dabbled around in making some web tools/WASM things, until I eventually had the thought: But what if I made a web port of Audacity? How hard could that be? Turns out: Browsers actually are reasonably capable at handling media, and the word robots are lying bastards which can be tamed somewhat by having enough tests.

And thus, Soundscaper exists now, featuring Audacity 4's UI, a bunch of extra features that Audacity doesn't have, and, going full circle, even desktop versions of it. And most importantly, it's owned by a non-profit, so I'll never again have to implement monetization strategies into an open source audio editor.

title.value: Show HN: Soundscaper – Audacity 4-like audio editor in the browser

Halo is privacy focused personal assistant for iOS that uses a custom built agent harness with support to use you existing LLM subscriptions, Wiki based memory system backed by on-device RAG, a full-fledged local browser agent, chat with generative UI and more.

TLDR: It's a better version of Hermes/OpenClaw for iOS, without needing a server! The better part is its proactive feature set and UX.

---

I started building Halo last year with 3 goals in mind: - Surface what’s important before I have to ask - Understand my life through the apps I already use - Keep my personal data on my device

Privacy is at the core of Halo and that's what sets it apart from other AI assistants. While other popular assistants on iOS save your private data such as emails, messages, etc on their servers, Halo stores all of it on your device.

I launched it today and have a 50% discount for the first week for early adopters. There is no subscription, just a single lifetime plan with a no-charge-at-end free trial. US price is $49 with PPP of up to 80% off for other countries like India.

More details here:

Read more about the memory system: https://meethalo.app/blog/how-halo-remembers/

X posts about building it publicly: https://x.com/search?q=from%3Atanmays%20halo

---

Please try it out, I promise it's not like any other AI assistant you tried and truly one of a kind iOS app. I spent more than a year building it. Would love to answer any questions you might have.

story_text.value:
When reading a history book, I sometimes have a hard time internalizing when the events are taking place. Sure, I know the dates, but it takes a bit of effort to put them in a broader context, to understand where in history they belong. What usually helps is to put them in relation to other contemporaneous events. To play around with this, I've made Meanwhile Map. You select a date and a time window, then scroll around the world map to see a list of contemporaneous events. For example, yes, the Mughal Empire was founded by Babur in the 1520s, but it paints a different picture in my head when I see that this roughly coincides with Cortés' capture of Tenochtitlan, or that it's close to the Siege of Vienna. Example link: https://meanwhilemap.com/#y=1520&m=1&span=120&off=founded,pe...

On the technical side, the app is a single static web page. It uses Wikidata for data (via SPARQL) and OpenHistoricalMap to show the events on the political map of the time. It's open source (https://github.com/ea/meanwhilemap/tree/main), vibe coded as an experiment. All processing is client-side, and no data is tracked other than simple visitor counts.

title.value: Show HN: Meanwhile Map – what else was happening in the world at the same time

story_text.value:
Hey HN! Sharing this script I've been using professionally and personally to stop the crazy influx of cold emails that I get daily.

It works in the following way:

1. Copy + install the Google Apps script in your Gmail. The script runs every 10 minutes by default.

2. The script will automatically use a series of Regexes as a first line of defense (modify as you like!). If that fails it will use an LLM of your choice to make the call (this is optional but highly effective).

3. Flagged emails skip the inbox and get tagged with a "Cold email" label. Nothing gets deleted.

From running this for the past couple of weeks, it catches 99% of all cold emails and helps me stay in flow state. Hope this helps other people too!

title.value: Show HN: A simple script to stop all cold sales emails from reaching your inbox

story_text.value:
I do a lot of work using claude and codex.

I use plenty of sub-agents. But nothing balances bang for the buck as good as deepseek v4.1 flash for me. So I thought, why not use the deepseek harness as MCP and drive it from claude as an orchestrator. I am probably not alone with this idea, but I haven't found something comparable. I wanted to fan out sub-agents and get back meaningful results.

Well, say hello to flash-agents.

With ollama as a backend driver no more training on my data (I think), and its pretty fast. I was driving a few billion tokens through that now without any issues. So I thought I'd open source it. What works for me, might work for others.

Let me know what you think. If you know anything better, always welcome. Not claiming my solution is yay, but it works for me so far, and I get real productivity gain out of it.
